topics.coverageNote: Based on NICE NG196 (individual recommendations carry year tags; no sourceYear stored), ACC/AHA 2023, AWMF 2025, SFNV/SFC 2024 and SCAI/HRS 2025. Topic is current.

mcqs.question: A 72-year-old man with AF has a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 and acceptable bleeding risk. What does NICE offer first-line?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) when CHA2DS2-VASc is 2 or above, taking bleeding risk into account.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer anticoagulation with a direct‑acting oral anticoagulant to people with atrial fibrillation and a CHA 2 DS 2 ‑VASc score of 2 or above, taking into account the risk of bleeding. Apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban and rivaroxaban are recommended as options, when used in line with the criteria specified in the relevant NICE technology appraisal guidance (see the section on direct-acting oral anticoagulant treatment options ). [2021]

mcqs.question: A patient with AF can't take DOACs because they are contraindicated. What does NICE offer instead?
mcqs.explanation: If DOACs are contraindicated, not tolerated or unsuitable, NICE offers a vitamin K antagonist.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If direct‑acting oral anticoagulants are contraindicated, not tolerated or not suitable in people with atrial fibrillation, offer a vitamin K antagonist. See the section on self-monitoring and self-management of vitamin K antagonists . [2021]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about aspirin monotherapy for stroke prevention in AF?
mcqs.explanation: NICE says not to offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention in AF.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention to people with atrial fibrillation. [2014]

mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman with AF has no risk factors other than her sex (CHA2DS2-VASc 1). What does NICE advise?

options.E: Offer a DOAC such as apixaban

mcqs.explanation: NICE does not offer anticoagulation to people under 65 whose only risk factor is sex (score 0 for men, 1 for women).

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer stroke prevention therapy with anticoagulation to people aged under 65 years with atrial fibrillation and no risk factors other than their sex (that is, very low risk of stroke equating to a CHA 2 DS 2 ‑VASc score of 0 for men or 1 for women). [ 2021]

mcqs.question: A patient's AF is no longer detectable after successful ablation. What does NICE advise about anticoagulation?

options.A: Stop it 3 months after the ablation
options.B: Stop it if a 12-lead ECG is normal
options.C: Don't stop it for that reason alone
options.D: Switch from a DOAC to aspirin
options.E: Halve the dose and review in a year

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Don't stop it for that reason alone
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises not stopping anticoagulation solely because AF is no longer detectable.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In people with a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation, do not stop anticoagulation solely because atrial fibrillation is no longer detectable. [2021]

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest considering left atrial appendage occlusion?

options.C: As a replacement for rate control
options.D: For all patients aged over 80 years
options.E: First-line as an alternative to DOACs

mcqs.explanation: NICE considers LAAO only if anticoagulation is contraindicated or not tolerated, and not as a routine alternative.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) if anticoagulation is contraindicated or not tolerated and discuss the benefits and risks of LAAO with the person. For more information see NICE's interventional procedure guidance on percutaneous occlusion of the left atrial appendage in non-valvular atrial fibrillation for the prevention of thromboembolism . [2014]
Do not offer LAAO as an alternative to anticoagulation unless anticoagulation is contraindicated or not tolerated. [2014]

mcqs.question: AF has lasted more than 48 hours and long-term rhythm control is planned. How long does NICE say therapeutic anticoagulation should be maintained before cardioversion?

options.B: None if a DOAC is used

mcqs.explanation: NICE delays cardioversion until at least 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation, with rate control in the meantime.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In people with atrial fibrillation in whom the duration of the arrhythmia is greater than 48 hours or uncertain and considered for long‑term rhythm control, delay cardioversion until they have been maintained on therapeutic anticoagulation for a minimum of 3 weeks. During this period offer rate control as appropriate. [2006, amended 2014]

mcqs.question: For AF persisting more than 48 hours, which type of cardioversion does NICE recommend?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers electrical rather than pharmacological cardioversion when AF has persisted for longer than 48 hours.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people having cardioversion for atrial fibrillation that has persisted for longer than 48 hours, offer electrical (rather than pharmacological) cardioversion. [2014]

mcqs.question: New-onset AF is to be cardioverted pharmacologically in a patient with structural heart disease. Which drug does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers amiodarone if there is structural heart disease. Flecainide or amiodarone can be chosen if there is no structural or ischaemic heart disease.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If pharmacological cardioversion has been agreed on clinical and resource grounds for new‑onset atrial fibrillation, offer: a choice of flecainide or amiodarone to people with no evidence of structural or ischaemic heart disease or amiodarone to people with evidence of structural heart disease. [2014]

mcqs.question: Which drug does NICE exclude from the 'standard beta-blocker' choice for initial rate control?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers a standard beta-blocker (other than sotalol) or diltiazem/verapamil as initial rate-control monotherapy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer either a standard beta‑blocker (that is, a beta‑blocker other than sotalol) or a rate‑limiting calcium‑channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) as initial rate‑control monotherapy to people with atrial fibrillation unless the person has the features described in recommendation 1.7.4. Base the choice of drug on the person's symptoms, heart rate, comorbidities and preferences. [2021] In April 2021, this was an off‑label use of diltiazem. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines .

mcqs.question: A patient presents acutely with AF and suspected acute decompensated heart failure. What does NICE advise about rate control?

options.A: Give IV verapamil for rapid rate control
options.C: Give diltiazem first-line for rate control
options.D: Give sotalol as the rate-control agent
options.E: Senior input on beta-blockers; no CCBs

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Senior input on beta-blockers; no CCBs
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises seeking senior specialist input before using beta-blockers and not using calcium-channel blockers in this situation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In people with atrial fibrillation presenting acutely with suspected concomitant acute decompensated heart failure, seek senior specialist input on the use of beta‑blockers and do not use calcium‑channel blockers. [2021]

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest considering digoxin monotherapy for initial rate control?

options.A: Paroxysmal AF in a trained athlete
options.D: All new-onset AF in the ED

mcqs.explanation: Digoxin monotherapy can be considered in non-paroxysmal AF if the person does little or no exercise, or other rate-limiting drugs are ruled out.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider digoxin monotherapy for initial rate control for people with non‑paroxysmal atrial fibrillation if: the person does no or very little physical exercise or other rate‑limiting drug options are ruled out because of comorbidities or the person's preferences. [2021]

mcqs.question: Which of these is an exception to NICE's rate-control-first strategy?

options.A: Permanent AF in an older person
options.B: AF with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 4
options.E: Heart failure caused by the AF

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Heart failure caused by the AF
mcqs.explanation: Exceptions include a reversible cause, heart failure primarily caused by AF, new-onset AF, flutter suitable for ablation, or when rhythm control is more suitable.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer rate control as the first‑line treatment strategy for atrial fibrillation except in people: whose atrial fibrillation has a reversible cause; who have heart failure thought to be primarily caused by atrial fibrillation; with new‑onset atrial fibrillation; with atrial flutter whose condition is considered suitable for an ablation strategy to restore sinus rhythm; for whom a rhythm‑control strategy would be more suitable based on clinical judgement. [2014]

mcqs.question: Which patient criteria does NICE require before considering a 'pill-in-the-pocket' strategy?
mcqs.explanation: Pill-in-the-pocket suits people with infrequent paroxysmal AF, no LV dysfunction or valvular/ischaemic disease, SBP >100 and resting HR >70.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In people with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation , a 'pill‑in‑the‑pocket' strategy should be considered for those who: have no history of left ventricular dysfunction, or valvular or ischaemic heart disease and have a history of infrequent symptomatic episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and have a systolic blood pressure greater than 100 mmHg and a resting heart rate above 70 bpm and are able to understand how to, and when to, take the medication. [2006]

mcqs.question: After left atrial ablation, what does NICE suggest considering to prevent recurrence?
mcqs.explanation: NICE suggests considering antiarrhythmic treatment for 3 months after left atrial ablation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider antiarrhythmic drug treatment for 3 months after left atrial ablation to prevent recurrence of atrial fibrillation, taking into account the person's preferences, and the risks and potential benefits. [2021]

mcqs.question: Symptomatic paroxysmal AF is refractory to at least one class I or III antiarrhythmic. What does ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS 2023 recommend?
mcqs.explanation: The 2023 guideline recommends catheter ablation for symptomatic paroxysmal AF refractory to at least one class I or III drug.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Catheter ablation is recommended for patients with symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation refractory to at least one Class I or III antiarrhythmic drug.

mcqs.question: Which scoring system does AWMF 2025 recommend for assessing thromboembolic risk in AF?
mcqs.explanation: AWMF 2025 recommends the CHA2DS2-VASc score, with oral anticoagulation indicated at a score of 2 or more.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The CHA2DS2-VASc score should be used to assess the risk of thromboembolic events in patients with atrial fibrillation.
Oral anticoagulation (OAC) is indicated in patients with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or higher, with the type of anticoagulant decided on an individual basis.

mcqs.question: What do SFNV/SFC 2024 recommend for patients with acute ischaemic stroke or TIA?
mcqs.explanation: The French societies recommend systematic AF screening after ischaemic stroke or TIA, and anticoagulation if AF is found.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Systematic screening for atrial fibrillation should be performed in all patients with acute ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack using coordinated multidisciplinary pathways.
Anticoagulant therapy should be initiated in patients with atrial fibrillation detected after ischaemic stroke or TIA as the primary prevention strategy to reduce recurrence risk.

mcqs.question: Symptomatic AF episodes are more than 24 hours apart. Which investigation does NICE suggest?
mcqs.explanation: For episodes more than 24 hours apart, NICE uses an ambulatory ECG monitor, event recorder or other ECG technology for an appropriate period.

sourceRefs.excerpt: use an ambulatory ECG monitor, event recorder or other ECG technology for a period appropriate to detect atrial fibrillation if symptomatic episodes are more than 24 hours apart. [2021]

mcqs.question: Anticoagulation has already been agreed on clinical criteria. What does NICE say about transthoracic echo?

options.A: Always do a TTE before starting a DOAC
options.B: Use TTE findings to choose the DOAC dose
options.C: Use TTE in place of the CHA2DS2-VASc score
options.D: Repeat TTE every 6 months on treatment
options.E: Don't do TTE just to stratify stroke risk

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Don't do TTE just to stratify stroke risk
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises not routinely performing TTE solely to further stratify stroke risk once anticoagulation has been agreed.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not routinely perform TTE solely for the purpose of further stroke risk stratification in people with atrial fibrillation for whom the need to start anticoagulation therapy has already been agreed on appropriate clinical criteria (see section 1.2 on assessment of stroke and bleeding risks and section 1.6 on stroke prevention). [2006, amended 2014]

topics.coverageNote: Pool combines bone metastases, palliative radiotherapy and radiotherapy principles. Mostly NICE NG234 spinal metastases/MSCC (2023 tags) and NICE brain tumours, plus trials and reviews from 2003–2024. Current.

mcqs.question: A patient has painful uncomplicated bone metastases. What do multiple stored sources say about single versus multiple fractions for pain relief?

options.A: SBRT is mandatory for all bone metastases
options.C: Single fraction is ineffective for pain
options.E: Multiple fractions give better pain relief

mcqs.explanation: RCR 2003, JCO 2007 and a 2024 review all report that single-fraction palliative radiotherapy relieves bone pain as well as multifraction.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
sourceRefs.excerpt: In the management of metastatic bone pain, single fraction radiotherapy is as effective as multifraction radiotherapy for pain relief.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
sourceRefs.excerpt: Single fractions (SFs) of palliative radiotherapy are comparable to multiple fractions (MFs) in terms of pain relief for painful bone metastases.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology
sourceRefs.excerpt: Single-fraction palliative radiotherapy is equally effective compared to multi-fractionated radiotherapy for relieving pain in patients with bone metastases, including in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

mcqs.question: What caveat about single-fraction radiotherapy for bone pain is noted in Clinical Oncology 2003?
mcqs.explanation: Clinicians should be aware of potentially higher re-treatment rates and uncertainty about preventing fracture and cord compression.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
sourceRefs.excerpt: When considering single fraction radiotherapy for metastatic bone pain, clinicians should be aware of potentially higher re-treatment rates and concerns regarding its efficacy in preventing future complications like pathological fracture and spinal cord compression, compared to multifraction radiotherapy.

mcqs.question: In the 2021 randomised trial, which regimen gave a better complete pain response than 20 Gy in 5 fractions?
mcqs.explanation: SBRT 24 Gy in 2 daily fractions was superior to 20 Gy in 5 fractions of conventional radiotherapy for complete pain response.

sourceRefs.excerpt: No treatment-related deaths were observed. Interpretation Stereotactic body radiotherapy at a dose of 24 Gy in two daily fractions was superior to conventional external beam radiotherapy at a dose of 20 Gy in five daily fractions in improving the complete response rate for pain. These results suggest that use of conformal, image-guided, stereotactically dose-escalated radiotherapy is approp

mcqs.question: What did a JAMA Network Open 2024 analysis conclude about SBRT for painful bone metastases?

options.A: Inferior to conventional EBRT for pain
options.C: Only useful when combined with surgery
options.D: Better complete pain response than cEBRT
options.E: Equivalent to cEBRT but more toxic

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Better complete pain response than cEBRT
mcqs.explanation: The 2024 analysis found SBRT more effective than conventional EBRT for achieving a complete pain response.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is more effective than conventional external beam radiotherapy (cEBRT) for achieving complete pain response in patients with painful bone metastases.

mcqs.question: MSCC is diagnosed and the patient isn't suitable for spinal surgery. How quickly does NICE say radiotherapy should start?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers urgent radiotherapy within 24 hours unless there has been complete paralysis for 2 weeks or more with controlled pain, or prognosis is poor.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer urgent radiotherapy (to be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours) to people with MSCC that is not suitable for spinal surgery, unless: they have had complete tetraplegia or paraplegia for 2 weeks or longer and their pain is well controlled or their overall prognosis is considered to be poor (see also the section on tools for assessing spinal stability and prognosis ). [2023]

mcqs.question: A patient has had complete paraplegia for 3 weeks from MSCC, their pain is well controlled, and surgery isn't suitable. What does NICE say about urgent radiotherapy?

options.A: It should be given with chemotherapy
options.B: It must still be given within 24 hours
options.C: It should be given before any steroids
options.D: It is an exception to the 24-h rule
options.E: It should be given within 1 hour

mcqs.correctAnswerText: It is an exception to the 24-h rule
mcqs.explanation: Complete tetraplegia or paraplegia for 2 weeks or longer with well-controlled pain is one of NICE's exceptions to urgent radiotherapy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer urgent radiotherapy (to be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours) to people with MSCC that is not suitable for spinal surgery, unless: they have had complete tetraplegia or paraplegia for 2 weeks or longer and their pain is well controlled or their overall prognosis is considered to be poor (see also the section on tools for assessing spinal stability and prognosis ). [2023]

mcqs.question: What imaging does NICE advise against for diagnosing or ruling out spinal metastases or MSCC?
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises not to do a plain spinal X-ray to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases or MSCC.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not do a plain X-ray of the spine to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases or MSCC. [2023]

mcqs.question: Spinal metastases are suspected without suspicion of MSCC. What MRI timing does NICE set?

options.B: Within 1 week at the local hospital
options.D: Within 24 hours at a tertiary centre

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Within 1 week at the local hospital
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers MRI within 1 week at the local hospital to guide treatment in suspected spinal metastases without suspected MSCC.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer an MRI scan to guide treatment options for people with clinical suspicion of spinal metastases but without suspicion of MSCC (see recommendation 1.3.3 ), to be done: within 1 week; at the local hospital. [2023]

mcqs.question: Dexamethasone was given before imaging, and spinal metastases and MSCC are then ruled out. What does NICE advise?
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises discontinuing dexamethasone if spinal metastases and MSCC are ruled out.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If dexamethasone is given before imaging, and spinal metastases and MSCC are subsequently ruled out, discontinue it. [2023]

mcqs.question: For which patients with spinal metastases does NICE suggest considering stereotactic ablative body radiotherapy?

options.C: Those unfit for any systemic therapy

mcqs.explanation: NICE considers SABR for people with good overall prognosis or oligometastases (up to 3 discrete metastases) with spinal involvement.

sourceRefs.excerpt: consider stereotactic ablative body radiotherapy for people with a good overall prognosis (see the section on tools for assessing spinal stability and prognosis ) or oligometastases (up to 3 discrete metastases anywhere in the body) with spinal involvement. [2023]

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest considering repeat radiotherapy for spinal metastases or MSCC?

options.B: Good prior response, relapse after 3+ months
options.D: Only if the previous dose was under 8 Gy
options.E: Only after failure of spinal surgery

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Good prior response, relapse after 3+ months
mcqs.explanation: Further radiotherapy can be considered after a good previous response with recurrent symptoms at least 3 months after the first course.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider further radiotherapy for people with spinal metastases or MSCC who have: had a good response to previous radiotherapy and developed recurrent symptoms at least 3 months after initial radiotherapy. [2023]

mcqs.question: What does NICE advise about radiotherapy after surgery for spinal metastases or MSCC?

options.D: Only if a pathological fracture occurs

mcqs.explanation: NICE offers postoperative radiotherapy once the person has recovered from surgery.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer postoperative radiotherapy after the person has recovered from surgery for spinal metastases or MSCC. For information on surgery, see the section on invasive interventions . [2023]

mcqs.question: A patient with prostate cancer has spinal metastases. When does NICE offer bisphosphonates for pain?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers bisphosphonates to reduce pain in prostate cancer spinal metastases only if conventional analgesia fails.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people with spinal metastases from prostate cancer, offer bisphosphonates to reduce pain only if conventional analgesia fails to control pain. [2008]

mcqs.question: A patient with a single brain metastasis has been treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. What does NICE advise about whole-brain radiotherapy?
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises not offering adjuvant WBRT after SRS, SRT or surgery for a single brain metastasis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer adjuvant whole-brain radiotherapy to people with a single brain metastasis treated with stereotactic radiosurgery or radiotherapy or surgery.

mcqs.question: A patient has NSCLC with brain metastases unsuitable for surgery or SRS, and a Karnofsky score of 60. What does NICE advise?
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises not offering WBRT in NSCLC brain metastases unsuitable for focal treatment when KPS is below 70.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer whole-brain radiotherapy to people with: non-small-cell lung cancer and brain metastases that are not suitable for surgery or stereotactic radiosurgery or radiotherapy and a Karnofsky performance status of under 70.

mcqs.question: A patient has multiple brain metastases, controlled extracranial disease and a Karnofsky score of 80. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: NICE considers SRS/SRT for multiple brain metastases with controlled extracranial disease and KPS of 70 or more, taking number and volume into account.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider stereotactic radiosurgery or radiotherapy for people with multiple brain metastases who have controlled or controllable extracranial disease and Karnofsky performance status of 70 or more. Take into account the number and total volume of metastases.

mcqs.question: What radiotherapy regimen does NICE offer for newly diagnosed glioblastoma in a patient aged around 70 or under with KPS 70 or more?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant temozolomide, then up to 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer radiotherapy using 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant temozolomide, followed by up to 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide, for people aged around 70 or under who have: a Karnofsky performance status of 70 or more and had maximal safe resection, or biopsy when resection is not possible, for a newly diagnosed grade 4 glioma (glioblastoma).

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest a baseline MRI after radiotherapy for glioma?
mcqs.explanation: NICE suggests considering a baseline MRI 3 months after radiotherapy for all types of glioma.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a baseline MRI scan 3 months after the completion of radiotherapy for all types of glioma.

mcqs.question: According to a Lancet Oncology 2017 analysis, which radiotherapy approach in head and neck SCC improved survival?
mcqs.explanation: Altered fractionation, particularly hyperfractionation, was associated with better overall and progression-free survival than conventional radiotherapy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, altered fractionation radiotherapy, particularly hyperfractionated radiotherapy, is associated with improved overall and progression-free survival compared to conventional radiotherapy.

mcqs.question: A patient with MSCC isn't suitable for surgery, radiotherapy or other oncology treatment. What does NICE advise about mobilisation?
mcqs.explanation: NICE states mobilisation should still be carried out if possible for these patients.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For a person with MSCC for whom surgery, radiotherapy or other oncology treatments are not appropriate, mobilisation should still be carried out if possible. [2023]

topics.coverageNote: Mostly NICE familial breast cancer (CG164; 2004/2013 tags) and familial ovarian cancer (NG241) recommendations, plus EHTG 2023/2024, JCO 2022 and other sources from 2019–2023. The pool is weighted towards breast/ovarian syndromes; only 2 items cover Lynch syndrome or polyposis.

mcqs.question: A woman with no personal history of cancer has a combined BRCA1/BRCA2 carrier probability of 12%, and her affected relative can't be tested. What does NICE advise?

options.C: Offer testing in a specialist clinic
options.D: Offer testing to the affected relative only

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Offer testing in a specialist clinic
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers testing in specialist genetic clinics when the combined BRCA1/2 probability is 10% or more and an affected relative is unavailable.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer genetic testing in specialist genetic clinics to a person with no personal history of breast or ovarian cancer if their combined BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carrier probability is 10% or more and an affected relative is unavailable for testing. [2013]

mcqs.question: A patient with invasive breast cancer has a 30% probability of a TP53 mutation. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: Offer genetic testing to guide treatment

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Offer genetic testing to guide treatment
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers genetic testing to people with invasive breast cancer or DCIS and a 30% TP53 mutation probability to help decide treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer people with invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ and a 30% probability of a TP53 mutation, genetic testing to help determine their treatment options. [2013]

mcqs.question: Which tool does NICE list for estimating the probability of a pathogenic variant?
mcqs.explanation: NICE lists the Manchester scoring system, CanRisk (BOADICEA), BRCAPRO or validated clinical criteria.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Genetics services should assess the probability of having a pathogenic variant using a calculation method with demonstrated accuracy, such as the Manchester scoring system, CanRisk (BOADICEA), BRCAPRO, or criteria based on specific clinical circumstances or a verified family history that are designed for the threshold used for testing.

mcqs.question: Under what circumstances does NICE support fast-track genetic testing (within 4 weeks of a breast cancer diagnosis)?

options.E: Only as part of a clinical trial

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Only as part of a clinical trial
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers fast-track genetic testing within 4 weeks of diagnosis only as part of a clinical trial.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer fast-track genetic testing (within 4 weeks of a diagnosis of breast cancer) only as part of a clinical trial. [2013]

mcqs.question: A high-risk predisposing mutation such as BRCA2 has been identified in a family. What does NICE advise for referral?
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises direct referral to a specialist genetics service when a high-risk mutation (for example BRCA1, BRCA2 or TP53) is identified.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Direct referral to a specialist genetics service should take place where a high-risk predisposing gene mutation has been identified (for example, BRCA1, BRCA2 or TP53). [2004]

mcqs.question: Where does NICE say a first- and second-degree family history should be taken for someone with breast symptoms and a family history concern?
mcqs.explanation: NICE takes a first- and second-degree family history in primary care. A third-degree history is taken in a specialist genetic clinic.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When a person with no personal history of breast cancer presents with breast symptoms or has concerns about relatives with breast cancer, a first- and second-degree family history should be taken in primary care to assess risk, because this allows appropriate classification and care. [2004]
A third-degree family history should be taken in a specialist genetic clinic for a person with no personal history of breast cancer, if this has not been done previously. [2004]

mcqs.question: A family includes a woman with triple-negative breast cancer diagnosed at age 36. What does NICE advise?

options.A: Repeat the family history in 5 years
options.B: No action, as one case is not enough
options.D: Refer to primary care for monitoring
options.E: Reassure and discharge to primary care

mcqs.explanation: NICE lists triple-negative breast cancer under 40 as a reason to seek further advice from specialist genetics services.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Clinicians should seek further advice from a specialist genetics service for families containing any of the following, in addition to breast cancers: triple negative breast cancer under the age of 40 years [2013]; Jewish ancestry [2004]; sarcoma in a relative younger than age 45 years [2004]; glioma or childhood adrenal cortical carcinomas [2004]; complicated patterns of multiple cancers at a young age [2004]; very strong paternal history (4 relatives diagnosed at younger than 60 years of age on

mcqs.question: Which populations does NICE say should be offered founder-variant testing for familial ovarian cancer, even without a family history?

options.B: All current or former smokers aged over 40
options.C: Anyone with benign breast cysts on imaging

mcqs.explanation: People with at least one grandparent from founder populations such as Ashkenazi Jewish should be offered genetic counselling and testing.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Recognise and raise awareness that people from the following populations (with at least 1 grandparent from the respective population), have a higher risk of having a founder pathogenic variant associated with familial ovarian cancer, so should be offered referral for genetic counselling and genetic testing for this variant, even if the person has no family or personal history of cancer: Ashkenazi Jewish; Sephardi Jewish; Greenlander. Also see the NHS Jewish BRCA Testing Programme , which offers

mcqs.question: According to EHTG/PLSD 2023, risk assessment in Lynch syndrome should be stratified by what?

options.E: The specific MMR gene and sex

mcqs.correctAnswerText: The specific MMR gene and sex
mcqs.explanation: Penetrance differs by MMR gene (MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, PMS2) and by sex, so management should be stratified accordingly.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: EHTG, PLSD (Hereditary cancer in clinical practice)
sourceRefs.excerpt: For dominantly inherited micro-satellite instable (MSI) cancers (the four Lynch syndromes), clinical management and risk assessment should be stratified by the specific mismatch repair (MMR) gene (MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, PMS2) and sex, as penetrance and expressivity differ significantly.

mcqs.question: According to JCO 2022, which approach shows promise for improving cascade testing uptake?

options.C: Direct contact of relatives by the team

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Direct contact of relatives by the team
mcqs.explanation: Direct relative contact by medical teams or testing laboratories showed promise over patient-mediated contact.

sourceRefs.excerpt: To improve uptake of cascade genetic counseling and testing for hereditary cancer syndromes, medical teams or testing laboratories should explore direct relative contact, while navigating privacy laws and infrastructure challenges, as it shows promise over patient-mediated contact.

mcqs.question: A woman is considering bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy. What does NICE recommend first?

options.B: Psychiatric assessment as the only step

mcqs.explanation: NICE recommends genetic counselling in a specialist cancer genetics clinic before a decision on bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Women considering bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy should have genetic counselling in a specialist cancer genetic clinic before a decision is made. [2004]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say clinical genetics laboratories should do with variants of uncertain significance?

options.A: Report them only to the patient's GP
options.C: Report them to patients as pathogenic
options.D: Record them in a searchable database
options.E: Withhold them from all medical records

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Record them in a searchable database
mcqs.explanation: Laboratories should record VUS and known pathogenic mutations in a searchable electronic database.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Clinical genetics laboratories should record gene variants of uncertain significance and known pathogenic mutations in a searchable electronic database. [2013]

mcqs.question: A direct-to-consumer test reports a BRCA pathogenic variant. What does NICE advise?
mcqs.explanation: Healthcare professionals should liaise with the regional NHS genetics service to discuss whether referral is appropriate.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If a person had a direct-to-consumer genetic test and is reported to have a pathogenic variant for which NHS testing is offered (for example, BRCA), healthcare professionals should liaise with the regional NHS genetics service to discuss whether referral is appropriate.

mcqs.question: Who does NICE make responsible for mainstream genetic testing in invasive epithelial ovarian cancer?
mcqs.explanation: The gynaecology oncology MDT is responsible for mainstream genetic counselling and testing for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The gynaecology oncology multidisciplinary team should be responsible for mainstream genetic counselling and genetic testing for people with invasive epithelial ovarian cancer.

mcqs.question: Risk-reducing surgery is being considered and no mutation has been found. What does NICE advise?

options.A: Test distant relatives before any decision
options.C: Repeat a risk score every year instead
options.D: Cancel the surgery until a mutation is found

mcqs.explanation: NICE advises confirming breast cancer-only histories via medical records, cancer registry or death certificates.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If substantial management decisions, such as risk-reducing surgery, are being considered and no mutation has been identified, clinicians should seek confirmation of breast cancer-only histories (via medical records/cancer registry/death certificates). [2004]

mcqs.question: What should be discussed with women who carry BRCA1 mutations about the oral contraceptive pill?

options.A: It has no effect on cancer risk
options.E: It is recommended for all carriers

mcqs.explanation: NICE asks for discussion of a potentially higher breast cancer risk under 40 against lifetime protection from ovarian cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For women with BRCA1 mutations, the conflicting effects of a potential increased risk of breast cancer under the age of 40 years and the lifetime protection against ovarian cancer risk from taking the oral contraceptive pill should be discussed. [2004]

mcqs.question: What does NICE offer everyone with breast cancer who is offered genetic testing?

options.A: The result given by telephone only
options.C: A letter to the GP with the result
options.E: A written leaflet with the result only

mcqs.explanation: NICE offers detailed consultation with a clinical geneticist or genetics counsellor, whatever the timeframe for testing.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer detailed consultation with a clinical geneticist or genetics counsellor to all those with breast cancer who are offered genetic testing, regardless of the timeframe for testing. [2013]

mcqs.question: What did a 2022 review recommend about managing hereditary cancer syndromes?

options.B: Focus only on the tested individual
options.E: Defer counselling until a cancer diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: The 2022 review recommends considering the impact on the whole family and supporting family adjustment.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: International journal of environmental research and public health
sourceRefs.excerpt: When managing hereditary cancer syndromes, healthcare providers should consider the impact on the entire family and support familial adjustment to genetic testing and risk management, rather than focusing solely on individual adjustment.

mcqs.question: Which group does NICE note may not come forward for ovarian cancer variant testing because they don't realise they're at risk?
mcqs.explanation: NICE notes that men, trans women and non-binary people born with male reproductive organs may not realise they could carry a relevant variant.

sourceRefs.excerpt: may not come forward for testing because they do not realise that they may be at risk of having a pathogenic variant associated with ovarian cancer (for example, men, trans women and non-binary people born with male reproductive organs).

mcqs.question: What does EHTG-ESCP 2024 advise for people with FAP or MAP?

options.B: Defer all care to primary care

mcqs.explanation: Updated European guidelines should be followed because of the higher lifetime risk of colorectal and other cancers in polyposis syndromes.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For individuals diagnosed with hereditary adenomatous polyposis syndromes (including FAP, MAP, GAPPS, and other rare adenomatous polyposis syndromes), updated European guidelines should be followed for clinical management to address the increased lifetime risk of colorectal and other cancers.

topics.coverageNote: Pool covers early, male and triple-negative breast cancer. Heavily weighted to NICE familial breast cancer risk management (CG164; 2004–2017 tags), plus ASCO 2017–2022, ACR 2025 and trials from 2017–2024. Treatment-specific depth is limited.

mcqs.question: A woman without breast cancer has taken chemoprevention for 5 years. What does NICE advise?

options.A: Double the dose for a further year
options.C: Switch to raloxifene for 5 more years

mcqs.explanation: NICE advises not continuing chemoprevention beyond 5 years in women with no personal history of breast cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not continue chemoprevention beyond 5 years in women with no personal history of breast cancer. [2013, amended 2017]

mcqs.question: A high-risk woman has had bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy. What does NICE say about chemoprevention?
mcqs.explanation: NICE says not to offer chemoprevention after bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer chemoprevention to women who were at high risk of breast cancer but have had bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy. [2013, amended 2017]

mcqs.question: A premenopausal woman at moderate risk with no thromboembolic or endometrial risk factors asks about chemoprevention. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: NICE suggests considering tamoxifen for 5 years in premenopausal women at moderate risk, unless they are at higher risk of thromboembolism or endometrial cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider tamoxifen for 5 years for premenopausal women at moderate risk of breast cancer, unless they have a past history or may be at increased risk of thromboembolic disease or endometrial cancer. [2017]

mcqs.question: A 40-year-old with treated breast cancer remains at high risk (BRCA2 carrier). What surveillance does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers annual MRI surveillance to women aged 30–49 with a personal history of breast cancer who remain at high risk.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer annual MRI surveillance to all women aged 30 to 49 years with a personal history of breast cancer who remain at high risk of breast cancer, including those who have a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation. [2013]

mcqs.question: A 55-year-old BRCA1 carrier with previous breast cancer (no TP53 mutation) asks about surveillance. What does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers annual mammographic surveillance to women aged 50–69 with a personal history who remain at high risk and don't have a TP53 mutation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer annual mammographic surveillance to all women aged 50 to 69 years with a personal history of breast cancer who: remain at high risk of breast cancer (including those who have a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation), and do not have a TP53 mutation. [2013]

mcqs.question: A 72-year-old high-risk woman with previous breast cancer (no TP53 mutation) asks about surveillance. What does NICE recommend?

options.B: Annual low-dose CT of the chest

mcqs.explanation: From age 70, NICE offers mammography as part of the population screening programme.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer mammography as part of the population screening programme for all women aged 70 years and over with a personal history of breast cancer who: remain at high risk of breast cancer (including those who have a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation), and do not have a TP53 mutation. [2013]

mcqs.question: What follow-up imaging does NICE offer all women with breast cancer?
mcqs.explanation: All women with breast cancer are offered annual mammography for 5 years of follow-up imaging.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Ensure that all women with breast cancer are offered annual mammography for 5 years for follow-up imaging, in line with the NICE guideline on early and locally advanced breast cancer . In conjunction with follow-up, women who remain at high risk of breast cancer and have a family history should receive surveillance as outlined in recommendations 1.6.11 to 1.6.15. [2013]

mcqs.question: An untested woman who was at more than 30% BRCA carrier probability reaches 60 without cancer. What does NICE say about MRI surveillance?
mcqs.explanation: Her carrier probability has now fallen below 30%, so MRI surveillance should no longer be offered.

sourceRefs.excerpt: High risk of breast cancer (untested but greater than 30% BRCA carrier probability) – surveillance recommendations reflect the fact that women who at first assessment had a 30% or greater BRCA carrier probability and reach 60 years of age without developing breast or ovarian cancer will now have a lower than 30% carrier probability and should no longer be offered MRI surveillance.

mcqs.question: A BRCA carrier with a uterus has had a premenopausal bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. What does NICE offer?

options.B: Tibolone only, for a maximum of 2 years
options.C: No HRT because of BRCA status

mcqs.explanation: NICE offers combined HRT if she has a uterus, or oestrogen-only HRT if not, until the expected age of natural menopause.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When women with no personal history of breast cancer have either a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation or a family history of breast cancer and they have had a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy before their natural menopause, offer them: combined HRT if they have a uterus; oestrogen-only HRT if they don't have a uterus up until the time they would have expected natural menopause (average age for natural menopause is 51 to 52 years). [2013]

mcqs.question: A woman with previous breast cancer has genitourinary menopause symptoms despite non-hormonal treatment. What does NICE suggest?
mcqs.explanation: NICE suggests considering vaginal oestrogen if symptoms continue despite non-hormonal treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider vaginal oestrogen for people with a personal history of breast cancer and genitourinary symptoms that have continued despite trying non-hormonal treatments (see also recommendation 1.5.16 for people receiving adjuvant aromatase inhibitor treatment for breast cancer). Vaginal oestrogen may be used in combination with a non-hormonal moisturiser or a lubricant. In November 2024, this was an off-label use of vaginal oestrogen. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines . [2024]

mcqs.question: What should women over 35 with a family history of breast cancer be told about the combined oral contraceptive pill?

options.A: It has no effect on breast cancer risk
options.B: It is linked to increased breast risk
options.D: It is contraindicated at any age

mcqs.correctAnswerText: It is linked to increased breast risk
mcqs.explanation: They should be told about a higher breast cancer risk with the pill, because their absolute risk increases with age.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Women aged over 35 years with a family history of breast cancer should be informed of an increased risk of breast cancer associated with taking the oral contraceptive pill, given that their absolute risk increases with age. [2004]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say women with a family history should be told about alcohol?

options.C: It has no effect on breast risk

mcqs.explanation: Alcohol may slightly increase breast cancer risk, balanced against other health effects.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Women with a family history should be informed that alcohol may increase their risk of breast cancer slightly. However, this should be considered in conjunction with any potential benefit of moderate alcohol intake on other conditions (such as heart disease) and adverse effects associated with excessive alcohol intake. [2004]

mcqs.question: Which family history qualifies for NICE referral to secondary care?

options.B: A first-degree male relative, any age
options.C: One aunt with breast cancer at 60
options.D: One cousin with ovarian cancer at 70

mcqs.correctAnswerText: A first-degree male relative, any age
mcqs.explanation: Criteria include a first-degree female relative diagnosed under 40, or a first-degree male relative at any age.

sourceRefs.excerpt: People without a personal history of breast cancer who meet the following criteria should be offered referral to secondary care: 1 first-degree female relative diagnosed with breast cancer at younger than age 40 years or 1 first-degree male relative diagnosed with breast cancer at any age or 1 first-degree relative with bilateral breast cancer where the first primary was diagnosed at younger than age 50 years or 2 first-degree relatives, or 1 first-degree and 1 second-degree relative, diagnosed

mcqs.question: According to ACR 2025, when is imaging appropriate as a screening test for breast cancer in men?

options.A: Annually for all men over 40 years
options.B: For all men with a family history
options.D: Not usually: average risk or under 25
options.E: Every 2 years for all men over 50

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Not usually: average risk or under 25
mcqs.explanation: ACR 2025 says imaging is usually not appropriate for screening average-risk men or men under 25.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For average-risk men and younger men less than 25 years of age, imaging is not usually appropriate as a screening test for breast cancer.

mcqs.question: What was the most common precursor lesion in male breast cancer in a 2017 study?
mcqs.explanation: DCIS was the most common precursor, and its presence was associated with better outcomes.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In conclusion, ductal carcinoma in situ is the most commonly observed precursor lesion in male breast cancer and its presence seems to be associated with a better outcome, in particular in Luminal B HER2+ cases.

mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of male breast problems, according to the 2018 source?
mcqs.explanation: Most male breast problems are benign, and gynaecomastia is the most common cause.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Although the majority of male breast problems are benign with gynecomastia as the most common etiology, men with breast symptoms and their referring providers are typically concerned about whether or not it is due to breast cancer. If the differentiation between benign disease and breast cancer cann

mcqs.question: Which genomic assay did ASCO 2017 endorse to guide adjuvant systemic therapy decisions in early breast cancer?
mcqs.explanation: ASCO 2017 states MammaPrint should be used to guide adjuvant systemic therapy decisions in early-stage invasive breast cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: MammaPrint (Agendia, Irvine, CA) should be used to guide decisions on the use of adjuvant systemic therapy for women with early-stage invasive breast cancer.

mcqs.question: What should be discussed before a risk-reducing mastectomy?

options.E: Cancer may be found on histology

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Cancer may be found on histology
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises discussing pre-operatively that breast cancer may be diagnosed histologically after a risk-reducing mastectomy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The possibility of breast cancer being diagnosed histologically following a risk-reducing mastectomy should be discussed pre-operatively. [2004]

mcqs.question: Why did ACOSOG (Alliance) need longer follow-up for the sentinel node metastasis trial?

options.B: Enrolment to the trial was slow

mcqs.explanation: Longer follow-up was needed because most tumours were oestrogen receptor-positive and may recur later.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Longer follow-up was necessary because the majority of the patients had estrogen receptor-positive tumors that may recur later in the disease course (the ACOSOG is now part of the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology). Objective To determine whether the 10-year overall survival of patients with sentinel lymph node metastases treated with breast-conserving therapy and sentinel lymph node

mcqs.question: Which question did the PALLAS trial investigate?
mcqs.explanation: PALLAS tested whether adding 2 years of palbociclib to adjuvant endocrine therapy improves invasive disease-free survival.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Background Palbociclib added to endocrine therapy improves progression-free survival in hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative, metastatic breast cancer. The PALLAS trial aimed to investigate whether the addition of 2 years of palbociclib to adjuvant endocrine therapy improves invasive dis
